answers.gloss: A supporting-TP is the adaptation/support relationship by which a client-layer TP is supported by a server-layer TP; it is not merely the lower-layer TP itself.
answers.example: An OTN termination point at R1 supported by an optical-layer termination point at R1.
answers.relations: It relates client and server termination points across adjacent layers and supports i.tp. The decisive experiment confirmed that it preserves the same adaptation-link identity and inter-layer relationship as t.translink.

answers.gloss: A tunnel termination point is the point where a TE tunnel originates or terminates—a trail head—not a generic external service-access point.
answers.example: The A1 trail head of the A1–A3 ODU2 tunnel.
answers.relations: It is located on i.tenode and originates or terminates i.tunnel; it identifies a tunnel endpoint at its head node.

answers.gloss: A TE tunnel is an end-to-end traffic-engineered path that realizes a service. It denotes the engineered tunnel itself, rather than the external service request, although it serves that request.
answers.example: The A1–A3 ODU2 tunnel engineered across the OTN topology.
answers.relations: It runs between i.ttp endpoints, traverses i.tetopo, contains or associates with i.tcep endpoints within nodes, and may be labeled by i.otnlabel.

answers.gloss: An OTN label represents the tributary-slot and tributary-port-number multiplexing allocation used to carry a lower-rate ODU within a higher-rate OTN container.
answers.example: The TS/TPN allocation carrying an ODU2 inside an OTU4.
answers.relations: It labels i.tunnel and expresses both the OTN multiplex structure and the concrete allocated switching resources, such as tributary slots.

answers.gloss: A tunnel connection endpoint is an endpoint of the tunnel's connection inside a node.
answers.example: The connection endpoint belonging to the A1–A3 tunnel on R1.
answers.relations: It is located on i.tenode and is part of i.tunnel. It is tunnel-specific, not a generic external service interface.

answers.gloss: An external, client-facing point where a requested service accesses the network; it is not a tunnel trail head.
answers.example: The ODU2 client hand-off at access node A1 for the A1–A3 service.
answers.relations: It is on t.node, provides access to t.cs, and marks the client/network boundary. It does not originate or terminate an internal TE tunnel as such.

answers.gloss: An externally meaningful end-to-end connectivity service, distinct from the engineered path or tunnel that realizes it.
answers.example: The requested A1–A3 ODU2 connectivity service.
answers.relations: It uses t.sip access points, is realized internally by connection endpoints t.cep, and operates over t.topo. It is the service object, not a combined service-and-path object.

answers.gloss: A qualifier describing the signal's layer and multiplexing structure, such as how a client ODU is mapped into a server container.
answers.example: ODU2 mapped into an OTU4 server signal.
answers.relations: It qualifies t.cs and expresses layer/multiplex structure. It does not identify a particular allocated tributary-slot or tributary-port-number resource.

answers.gloss: An endpoint of a service-realizing connection within a node.
answers.example: The connection endpoint for the A1–A3 service on R1.
answers.relations: It is located on t.node and is part of, or realizes, t.cs. It is connection-specific, but model A associates it directly with the connectivity service rather than explicitly with a separately represented TE tunnel.
